plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the geometry of light refraction at a planar interface between two optical media, as described by Snell's law. A horizontal black line divides the scene into an upper region with refractive index n1 and a lower region with refractive index n2; a thick blue line traces the ray direction as it strikes the interface and continues into the second medium. A thin vertical line marks the surface normal at the point of incidence, with a small right-angle square confirming its perpendicularity to the interface; the angle theta_1 is measured between the incoming ray and the normal above the interface, and theta_2 is measured between the refracted ray and the normal below. The ray bends toward or away from the normal depending on the relative magnitudes of n1 and n2, embodying the relationship n1 sin theta_1 = n2 sin theta_2. This figure introduces refraction geometry as the physical basis for how lenses bend light and form images.

interactionPlan.concept: At a planar boundary between two media, a light ray bends so that n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ — toward the normal when entering a denser medium, away when entering a rarer one, and reflecting entirely once θ₁ exceeds the critical angle.
elements: Horizontal thick black line spanning the full width: the planar interface between the two media
Upper half-plane region labeled 'n₁' (left side, above the interface)
Lower half-plane region labeled 'n₂' (left side, below the interface)
Thin light-blue vertical line through the incidence point: the surface normal, extending both above and below the interface
Text label 'surface normal' at the top of the normal line
Small black right-angle square at the intersection of normal and interface (upper-right quadrant) marking perpendicularity
Thick blue incident ray coming from upper-left down to the incidence point, with label 'ray direction' written along the ray
Thick blue refracted ray continuing from the incidence point into the lower medium
Angle arc and label 'θ₁' between the incident ray and the upward normal
Angle arc and label 'θ₂' between the refracted ray and the downward normal
Dashed/secondary blue reflected ray in the upper medium, mirrored about the normal (appears when total internal reflection occurs, or shown faintly as the partial reflection)
Numeric readout panel showing θ₁, θ₂, n₁, n₂ and the products n₁sin θ₁ and n₂sin θ₂
Annotation text 'Total internal reflection' with the critical angle value, shown when θ₁ ≥ θ_c
Small filled dot marking the point of incidence

interactions.teaches: The ray pivots about the incidence point: as the incoming ray is swung, θ₂ responds continuously but never in proportion — it is the sines, not the angles, that stay locked in ratio.

demo_steps.title: Normal incidence: no bending
demo_steps.narration: With the ray straight down the normal, θ₁ = 0 and θ₂ = 0 — a ray hitting the surface head-on passes through undeviated no matter what the indices are.

demo_steps.title: Entering a denser medium bends toward the normal
demo_steps.narration: Tilt the ray to 40°. Because n₂ > n₁, the refracted ray makes a smaller angle with the normal: sin θ₂ = (n₁/n₂) sin θ₁, so θ₂ ≈ 25°.

demo_steps.title: Raising n₂ bends the ray even harder
demo_steps.narration: Push n₂ up toward 2.4 (diamond) while holding θ₁ fixed. The refracted ray swings closer to the normal — the stronger the index contrast, the sharper the bend.

demo_steps.title: Reversing the contrast bends away from the normal
demo_steps.narration: Now make the upper medium the dense one (n₁ = 1.5, n₂ = 1.0). The refracted ray swings away from the normal, flattening toward the surface.

demo_steps.title: Past the critical angle: total internal reflection
demo_steps.narration: Keep n₁ > n₂ and push θ₁ past θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁) ≈ 42°. Snell's law would demand sin θ₂ > 1, which is impossible — the refracted ray vanishes and all the light reflects back, mirrored about the normal.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Refraction conserves n·sin θ across the boundary, not the angle itself — which is why a bigger index means a smaller angle, and why the light has nowhere to go but back when n₁ sin θ₁ exceeds n₂.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Clean white background, hand-drawn textbook feel. A thick black horizontal interface line spans the full width at mid-height. 'n₁' sits above-left of it and 'n₂' below-left, in large serif type. A thin cyan vertical line (the surface normal) crosses the interface slightly right of center, labeled 'surface normal' at its top. A small black right-angle square sits in the upper-right corner of the normal/interface intersection. The incident ray is a thick saturated blue line entering from the upper-left at a steep angle down to the intersection point, with 'ray direction' lettered along it; the refracted ray continues below the interface in the same thick blue, bent toward the normal when n₂ > n₁. Thin arcs near the normal carry the labels θ₁ (above) and θ₂ (below). A lighter blue dashed ray mirrored about the normal into the upper-left→upper-right direction represents reflection; it becomes solid and prominent under total internal reflection, at which point the lower blue ray disappears and a red-orange 'Total internal reflection (θ_c = …)' caption appears near the interface. A small corner readout lists n₁, n₂, θ₁, θ₂ and the two equal products n₁sin θ₁ and n₂sin θ₂ so the invariant is visible while dragging.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Drag the incident ray to change θ₁ and watch θ₂ update in real time according to n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with both angle arc labels refreshing as the ray rotates about the interface point
- Sliders for refractive indices n₁ and n₂: show how increasing n₂ relative to n₁ bends the refracted ray closer to the surface normal, and vice versa
- Increase n₁ above n₂ and drag θ₁ past the critical angle to trigger total internal reflection, showing the refracted ray disappear below the interface and a reflected ray appear symmetrically above it

discrepancies: Source has no angle arcs, no point-of-incidence dot, and no numeric readout box; the generated figure adds arcs, a dot marker, and a stats panel in the lower-left, which adds clutter not in the original.

The 'ray direction' text in the source sits above/left of the incident ray far from the origin; here it is placed closer to the ray mid-point and overlaps the ray's stroke region, reading slightly cramped.
The n₁/n₂ labels render as 'n1'/'n2' (subscript glyphs not rendering in the serif font at that size), losing the subscript typography of the source.

Interface line and normal extents differ: in the source the normal stops well short of the canvas bottom/top asymmetrically and the black interface spans the full width; the generated interface line is noticeably shorter relative to the drawing area.
θ₂ label in the source sits left of the refracted ray near the normal; generated θ₂ is placed further out and further down, and θ₁ sits closer to the vertex than in the source.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and pedagogically strong Snell's-law figure with correct geometry, colors and working sliders/drag/guided-tour interactions; main weaknesses are added non-source chrome (readout box, angle arcs, vertex dot) and subscript glyphs failing to render in the n₁/n₂ labels.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are implementation details (subscript glyph rendering, extra chrome like the readout box/arcs/dot, and label placement/line extents) that belong to the generator.

intro
Snell: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Hover any element for a hint; click for an explanation.

discrepancies: Incident/refracted ray stroke is slightly thinner and a deeper navy (#0026E6) than the pure, very heavy blue of the source; the normal is also a touch thicker relative to the source's thin cyan line.
The 'ray direction' text in the source is drawn in a lighter hand-lettered style slightly further up the ray; here it sits closer to the intersection and uses a serif face — a cosmetic drift only.
The θ₂ label sits a little closer to the normal / higher up than in the source, where it is farther down and nearer the refracted ray.
Checkbox controls in the UI panel render with the box on a separate line above its text label, which reads awkwardly (usability nit, not a figure-content error).
evaluation.notes: Default state is an excellent drop-in replacement for the source refraction diagram (thick blue bent ray, cyan normal, right-angle square, n₁/n₂, θ₁/θ₂, 'ray direction', 'surface normal'), and the added sliders, drag-the-ray handle, reflected-ray/measurement toggles and 5-step Snell's-law tour are correct and pedagogically strong; only minor stylistic/label-placement drift and a cosmetic checkbox layout issue detract.

feedback.rationale: No failure modes or action items remain and all core dimensions score 5 with only cosmetic styling drift, so the figure is good enough to stop iterating.
